title: Use informal arguments to find angle relationships with parallel lines and triangles

steps.text: I can find missing angles where two lines cross.
steps.example: Lines cross at 58°: the angle beside it is 122°, across is 58°.

steps.text: I can tell if two angles at parallel lines are equal or add to 180°.
steps.example: Same-side interior angles: 70° and 110° add to 180°.

steps.text: I can find the missing angle in a triangle.
I can find a triangle's outside angle from the two far inside angles.
steps.example: Far inside angles 38° and 81° → outside angle = 119°

steps.text: I can use two matching angles to tell if triangles are similar.
steps.example: Both triangles have 104° and 44° angles → similar (AA).

steps.text: I can write and solve an equation using one or more angle rules.
I can find and fix a mistake in someone's angle work.
steps.example: Same-side angles add to 180°, not equal: 8x + 20 = 180, x = 20

steps.text: I can explain why a triangle's angles always add to 180°.
steps.example: Draw a parallel line at the top: the 3 angles fill a straight line, 180°.

title: Explain a proof of the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse

steps.text: I can name the legs and the hypotenuse of a right triangle.
steps.example: The hypotenuse is the longest side, across from the right angle.

steps.text: I can write a² + b² = c² for a right triangle.
I can show the two leg squares add up to the hypotenuse square.
steps.example: Leg squares 25 cm² + 144 cm² → hypotenuse square 169 cm²

steps.text: I can use the converse to test if three sides make a right triangle.
I can find and fix a mistake in a right-triangle test.
steps.example: Wrong: 7² + 25² = 24². Fix: c is longest, so 7² + 24² = 25² ✓

steps.text: I can use a picture of squares to explain why a² + b² = c².
I can tell when to use the theorem and when to use its converse.
steps.example: Find a missing side: theorem. Check for a right angle: converse.

title: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find unknown side lengths in right triangles in 2D and 3D

steps.text: I can tell that a² + b² = c² only works for right triangles.
steps.example: A triangle with no 90° angle: a² + b² = c² does not work.

steps.text: I can find the hypotenuse when I know both legs.
I can find a missing leg when I know the hypotenuse.
I can give a side as a square root and round it to tenths.
I can draw and label a right triangle to solve a word problem.
steps.example: 17-ft ladder, base 8 ft out: 8² + h² = 17², h = 15 ft

steps.text: I can solve a problem when a side is given as a square root.
I can use a² + b² = c² twice to solve a 3D problem.
steps.example: Box 16 × 12 × 15 in: floor diagonal 20, corner to corner 25

steps.text: I can simplify a square root answer.

title: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find the distance between two points in a coordinate system

steps.text: I can find how far apart two points are across and up or down.
I can draw a right triangle that connects two points on a grid.
steps.example: A(−4, −1), B(4, 5): corner C(4, −1); AB is the hypotenuse

steps.text: I can use a² + b² = c² to find the distance between two points.
I can find a distance that is not a whole number and round it.
I can find the length of a rectangle's diagonal on a grid.
I can solve a problem that needs more than one distance.
I can explain the steps I used to find a distance.
steps.example: I drew a right triangle, legs 6 and 8, so d = √100 = 10.

steps.text: I can find the distance between two points in 3D.

title: Describe the effect of translations, reflections, rotations, and dilations on 2D figures using coordinates

steps.text: I can translate (slide) a point with a rule like (x − 5, y + 3).
I can reflect (flip) a point across the x-axis or the y-axis.
I can rotate (turn) a point 90° or 180° around the origin.
I can dilate (resize) a point from the origin by a scale factor.
I can find the scale factor of a dilation from the coordinates.
I can name the one move that maps a figure onto its image.
I can find and fix a mistake in a coordinate rule.
I can do a set of moves with a dilation and tell what changed.
I can tell how a dilation changes a figure's area.

title: Understand congruence through rotations, reflections, and translations

steps.text: I can explain that slides, flips, and turns keep size and shape the same.
steps.example: After a turn, GH = 7 cm, so G′H′ = 7 cm.

steps.text: I can graph a figure after one slide, flip, or turn.
steps.example: Slide left 3: (2, 4) → (−1, 4); plot each new point.

steps.text: I can match the sides and angles of two congruent figures.
I can use congruent figures to find a missing side.
I can find a set of moves that maps one figure onto another.
steps.example: Flip over the x-axis, then slide (x − 6, y + 1).

steps.text: I can prove two figures are congruent using slides, flips, and turns.
steps.example: A flip, then a slide, lands △ABC on △DEF. Both rigid, so ≅.

steps.text: I can choose the shortest set of moves that works.
steps.example: Flip over x-axis, then y-axis = one 180° turn; the turn is shortest.

title: Understand similarity through dilations and sequences of transformations

steps.text: I can explain that a dilation keeps angles the same and multiplies every side.
steps.example: Dilate by 1.5: side 6 → 9; a 90° angle stays 90°.

steps.text: I can find the scale factor between two similar figures.
I can match parts of similar figures and write a similarity statement.
I can check if two figures are similar by comparing side ratios.
steps.example: 6/4 = 1.5 and 15/10 = 1.5, so the rectangles are similar.

steps.text: I can use a proportion to find a missing side in similar figures.
I can tell if a set of moves makes a congruent or a similar figure.
steps.example: Slide, then turn: congruent. Dilate by 4, then slide: similar.

steps.text: I can prove two figures are similar with moves that include a dilation.
steps.example: Dilate by 3, then turn 90°: △ABC lands on △DEF, so similar.

steps.text: I can use similar triangles to measure something too tall to reach.
steps.example: 5-ft boy, 4-ft shadow; tree shadow 36 ft → tree is 45 ft

title: Know and use the formulas for the volumes of cylinders, cones, and spheres

steps.text: I can find the radius and height of a cylinder or cone, and a sphere's radius.
steps.example: Can with diameter 8 cm, height 11 cm: r = 4 cm

steps.text: I can find the volume of a cylinder with V = πr²h.
I can find a cone's volume: ⅓ of the matching cylinder.
I can find the volume of a sphere with V = (4/3)πr³.
I can give a volume in terms of π or rounded, in cubic units.
I can find and fix mistakes like using the diameter as the radius.
steps.example: Cone, d = 12, h = 10: use r = 6, V = 120π

steps.text: I can find a missing radius or height when I know the volume.
steps.example: Cone 48π ft³, h = 9: 3πr² = 48π, so r = 4 ft

steps.text: I can find the volume of a solid made of two or more shapes.
I can explain why changing the radius changes volume more than the height.
steps.example: Triple r: volume ×9, since r is squared. Triple h: only ×3.
